﴿Has your Lord then preferred you with sons and taken from the angels females?﴾ — chosen you and singled you out. ﴿Indeed you are saying a grave saying﴾: addressing the polytheists of the Arabs, when they said: the angels are the daughters of God.

﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an﴾: the common readers read it with shadd on the ṣād, for intensification. al-Ḥasan read ṣarafnā with tashdīd removed.

﴿In this Qur'an﴾: meaning the lessons, wisdoms, parables, rulings, proofs and signs.

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Ḥusayn say, in the presence of the Imam Abu al-Ṭayyib, regarding His saying ṣarrafnā, that it has two meanings. The first: He did not make it one kind, but rather promise and warning, command and prohibition, decisive and ambiguous, abrogating and abrogated, reports and parables, like the diversification of winds: east, west, south and north; and the diversification of verbs from past to future, from active to passive, and the like.

The second: He did not reveal it once, but in installments (nujūman), as in His saying ﴿And a Qur'an We have divided (farraqnāhu)﴾, meaning: We have repeatedly turned Gabriel toward you. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/265.]]

﴿That they may remember (liyadhdhakkarū)﴾. Yaḥyā, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read liyadhkurū without shadd. The rest read it with shadd, and Abu ʿUbayd chose it, meaning: that they may take heed (liyatadhakkarū). ﴿And it increases them only in aversion﴾: fleeing and distancing from the truth.

﴿Say, O Muhammad, to these polytheists: if there were with Him other gods, as they say﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ḥafṣ read yaqūlūna with ya'; the rest with ta'.

﴿Then they would have sought to the Lord of the Throne a way﴾: they would have sought the gods to draw near to Him, seeking nearness to Him.

Qatada said: It means: if the matter were as they say, then they would know God's favor and His nearness to them, so they would do what draws them closer to Him.

Others said: then they would have sought, along with God, contention and fighting, like the kings of the world acting against one another. Then He declared Himself free of what they say, saying ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted far above what they say﴾.

al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i, and Abu ʿUbayd chose it from them, read ta'ālā with the tā' ("ʿulūwan kabīran"), great exaltation, and did not say ta'āliyan, like His saying [wa-ja'ala] to Him a way.

﴿And give the near of kin his due﴾. This means maintaining ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim).

Some said: it refers to the kinship of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Al-Suddi narrated from Ibn al-Daylami who said: ʿAli ibn al-Husayn said to a man from the people of Syria, "Have you recited the Qur'an?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Have you not read in (the chapter of) the Children of Israel: ﴿And give the near of kin his due﴾?" He said, "Are you the near of kin whom God commanded to be given their due?" He said, "Yes."

﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾: the traveller on the road. It was also said: the guest.

﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾: do not spend your wealth in disobedience.

Salama ibn Kuhayl narrated from Abu [ʿUbayda], from Ibn al-Ḍarīr, that he asked Ibn Masʿud, "What is wastefulness (tabdhīr)?"

He said: "Spending wealth in other than its right place." [[Tafsir Mujahid: 1/361.]]

Mujahid said: If a person spent all his wealth in what is right, it would not be wastefulness; but if he spent a single hand's worth in what is false, that would be wastefulness.

Shuʿayb said: I was walking with Abu Ishaq on the road to Kufa when he came upon a house being built with plaster and baked brick, and he said: "This is wastefulness, according to the saying of ʿAbd Allah: spending wealth in other than its right place." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/94.]]

﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾: their helpers and allies. The Arabs say: whoever adheres to the custom of a people and follows their way is their brother. ﴿And Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾: denying the blessings.

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾, the verse.

It was revealed concerning Munajji, Bilal, Suhayb, Salim and Khabbab. They used to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) from time to time for what they needed, and he did not find anything to give them, so he would turn away from them out of shyness before them.

Then God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾, meaning: if you turn away from these people to whom I ordered you to give their rights when they ask you, and you have nothing to give them, out of shame before them.

﴿Seeking mercy from your Lord﴾: seeking provision from God, which you hope will come to you. ﴿Then speak to them a gentle word﴾: softly, promising them a good promise.

﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, the verse.

Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah said: While the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sitting among the Companions, a boy came to him and said, "O Messenger of God, my mother asks you to clothe her with a garment." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had nothing but his shirt. The boy said, "From one hour to another, it appears there is a delay until another time." So he went back to his mother, who said, "Tell him: my mother asks you for the garment you are wearing." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered his house, took off his shirt, gave it to him, and sat naked. Bilal called the adhan for the prayer, and they waited, but he did not come out. This troubled the hearts of the Companions, so some of them entered upon him and saw him naked. Then God, Exalted, revealed: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾. [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 194.]]

Meaning: do not withhold your hand from spending in what is right, like a hand bound to the neck, which cannot be extended to give.

﴿Nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ in giving, so that you give all that you possess, ﴿and so you sit reproached﴾: your askers will blame you when you do not give them, ﴿and destitute﴾: cut off from you, with nothing left to spend. It is said: "He was exhausted (ḥasara) by the request," when it wearied him. A beast is ḥasīr when it is weary and exhausted. And ḥasīr of sight is when it is tired. God said: ﴿Your sight will return to you dazzled while it is weary﴾ [Surat al-Mulk: 4]. Qatada said: regretful for what has passed from you. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/251.]]

﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾: He widens and narrows. ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿If God had extended provision to His servants, they would have committed excess upon the earth﴾, the verse. [Here the text reads "wa-law wassaʿa" as in the manuscript.]

﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾: destitution and scarcity. ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾. This was because the people of ignorance used to bury their daughters alive for fear of poverty, so God forbade them from that and informed them that their provision and the provision of their daughters is upon God, Exalted. ﴿Indeed, their killing has ever been a great sin﴾. The readers differed concerning it:

Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fatḥa on the kha and the ṭāʾ, with the hamza shortened (khiṭʾan).

Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra on the kha, a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ, and a long hamza (khiṭāʾan).

The rest read it with a kasra on the kha and a sukūn on the ṭāʾ (khiṭan). All these are dialectal forms with one meaning, and the word may be a noun or a verbal noun.

﴿And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse; indeed it is ever an immorality and an evil way﴾.

﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾: and by its right, which is what [follows].

Humayd narrated from Anas who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say: there is no god but God. When they say it, their blood and their property are protected from me, except by its right, and their reckoning is with God." It was said: What is its right? He said: "Adultery after being married, apostasy after faith, and killing a soul, so that he is killed in retaliation for it." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/103.]]

﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾: power and authority over the killer of his heir. If he wishes, he may take retaliation; if he wishes, he may pardon him; if he wishes, he may take blood money, which God has made lawful. ﴿But let him not commit excess in killing﴾. Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with the letter ta' (tusrif), meaning: do not commit excess, O killer. It is also possible that the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), with the intended meaning being the leaders and the community after him. Whoever reads it with ya' refers it to the heir (al-mawlā).

They differed about what excess is. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he should not kill anyone other than his killer.

al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: In the days of ignorance, when one of the Arabs was killed, they would not be content to kill the killer of their companion until they had killed someone more noble than the one who had killed him. So the heir of the victim would go to a noble man of the killer's tribe and kill him in exchange for his heir, leaving the killer alive. God forbade this.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among the people most defiant toward God, may He be praised, is one who kills someone other than his killer, or who kills in the manner of the ignorance of the Jahiliyya, or who kills in the sanctuary of God." [[Ibid.: 15/106.]]

al-Ḍaḥḥak said: This was in Mecca while the Prophet of God (ﷺ) was there, and it was the first thing revealed from the Qur'an concerning killing. The polytheists of Mecca were killing the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). God said: whoever among the polytheists kills you, let his killing you not lead you to kill none but your killer; so do not kill, for the sake of him, a father, a brother, or anyone; if they are from the polytheists, let that not lead you to [...] [unreadable text] so do not kill except your killer. [As in the manuscript.]

This was before Surat Bara'a was revealed and before they were commanded to fight the polytheists.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: it is not accepted [...] upon the number [of killings].

Qatada, Ṭāriq ibn Ḥabīb and Ibn Kaysan said: [the victim] is not to be mutilated.

﴿Indeed he was supported﴾: scholars differed about to whom this pronoun refers. It was said it refers to the heir of the victim: he is the one supported against the killer, so the ruler hands the killer over to him; if he wishes he kills him, if he wishes he pardons him, if he wishes he takes the blood money. This is the view of Qatada.

Others said: the pronoun "whoever" [man] refers to the victim in His saying ﴿and whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, meaning that the victim is supported in this world by retaliation, and in the Hereafter by repentance. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan, except in the best manner until he reaches maturity﴾... [the verse continues] ﴿and fulfil the covenant; indeed the covenant is ever questioned﴾ about it. It was also said its meaning is: it was wrongful.

﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even balance﴾.

The people of Kufa read al-qisṭās with a kasra on the qāf. The rest read it with a fatḥa, and it means the balance, like al-qirṭās. Al-qisṭās means a balance, whether small or large. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/257.]]

Mujahid said: it is justice in Greek (rūmiyya). al-Ḥasan said: it is the steelyard (al-qabbān).

﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome﴾: that is, in its consequence.

[al-Ḥasan said:] It has been related to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: "No man has power over something forbidden and then leaves it, having nothing but fear of God, except that God will replace it for him in the hasty world before the Hereafter with something better for him than that." [[Kanz al-ʿUmmal: 15/787; Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/109.]]

﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾. Qatada said: do not say "I saw" when you did not see, or "I heard" when you did not hear, or "I know" when you do not know. This is a report from ʿAli from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Mujahid said: do not accuse anyone of what you have no knowledge of. This is the narration of ʿAṭiyya from Ibn ʿAbbas. [[See Zad al-Masir of Ibn al-Jawzi: 5/27.]]

Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya said: it is false testimony.

[al-Qutaybi] said: do not follow conjecture and assumptions. All of these are close in meaning. The root of qafw is slander and false accusation. From it comes the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We are the sons of al-Naḍr ibn Kinana; we do not slander our mother, nor do we disown our father." [[al-Mu'jam al-Kabir of al-Tabarani: 1/236; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 1/22, with the wording: "nor do we claim (to be) of other than our father".]]

al-Nabigha said:

"And like statues, of noble noses, dwelling
with them is modesty; they do not wrong with accusations (al-taqāfī)."
[al-Taqafi: accusing, the verse is attributed in Tafsir al-Tabari to some Basran scholars: 15/110.]

al-Kumayt said:

"So I do not hurl at the innocent without fault,
nor do I slander the chaste, when we were slandered."
[As in the manuscript.]

[al-Qutaybi] said: it is derived from the qafa' (back of the head), as if one follows (yaqfū) matters and goes after their backs, and follows them and seeks to know them. It is said: "I followed his trace" (qafawtu athārahu), on the pattern of "I called" (daʿawtu). Its prohibition is: do not follow (lā taqfu), like your saying: do not leave (lā tadaʿ).

al-Farra' related from some people that its origin is from al-qiyafa, which is following a trace. If that is so, then (wa-lā taqfu) must be read with a ḍamma on the qāf and a sukūn on the fā', like (wa-lā taqul). He said: The Arabs say: "I followed her trace" and "I followed (qafat)" like their saying: qā'a al-jamal al-nāqa idhā rakibahā waqʿan (the camel mounted the she-camel), and ʿāth and ʿathan, iʿtāma and iʿtamā, and iḥtāja māluhu and iḥtajā.

The poet said:

"And if I had struck you from close by,
it would have pulled you away from the wolf's cry, the wolf."

That is, it embraced (ʿānaqa). [As in the manuscript.]

﴿Indeed the hearing and the sight and the heart, all of those﴾: that is, all these limbs and organs, will be asked about those [acts].

As in the saying of the poet, Jarir:

"Blame the dwellings after the place of al-Liwā,
and life after those days."
[See Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/111.]

It may also be that the pronoun refers to their owners and possessors.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾: with arrogance, pride and vanity. This explains the walking, not describes it, because this emphasis is put in the form of the verbal noun. ﴿Indeed you will never tear the earth﴾: that is, you will never cut it with your heels until you reach its end. It is said: "So-and-so is more the tearer of the earth than so-and-so" when he travels more and is stronger.

Ruʾba said:

"And a standing one, of the depths, empty of the cut-through"
meaning: the one cut off.

﴿Nor will you reach the mountains in height﴾: that is, you will not equal them in height, nor will your stature reach them. He informed that whoever does this gains nothing from it [...] [unreadable word] from him anything else. ﴿All that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾.

al-Ḥasan, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn ʿUmar and the people of Kufa read sayyi'uhu as an annexed construction (iḍāfa), meaning: all this which we have mentioned, from His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾.

[The reading] "kāna sayyiʾatan" means "it was an evil thing," in respect of what we have mentioned and promised concerning you. ﴿In the sight of your Lord, hateful.﴾ They said: because in what God has mentioned, from His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ up to this point, there are things commanded and things forbidden. Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading for the meaning mentioned, and because in the reading of Abu Ḥajja, which Abu ʿUbayd related from Ḥajjāj from Hārūn, in the reading of [Ubayy ibn Kaʿb]: (kāna sayyi'ātuhu), he said: this would be by annexing an indefinite accusative sayyi'a, meaning: all that which we have mentioned and promised from His saying ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ up to this point was an evil thing, not a good thing. So they made "kull" comprehensive of what is forbidden and nothing else. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/262.]]

If it is said: why did you not make makrūhan a second predicate? We say: there is a fronting and deferment in the speech; its intended sense is: all that was hateful and evil. It was said: it is an act [...] like a substitute, not as a description; the meaning: all that was evil and was hateful.

The people of Kufa said: it refers to meaning, because sayyi'a is a sin, and it is [not literal]. ﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾, up to His saying ﴿dismissed﴾: cast out, banished from every helper. The intended meaning is other than him.

They differed about what excess is. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he should not kill anyone other than his killer.

al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: In the days of ignorance, when one of the Arabs was killed, they would not be content to kill the killer of their companion until they had killed someone more noble than the one who had killed him. So the heir of the victim would go to a noble man of the killer's tribe and kill him in exchange for his heir, leaving the killer alive. God forbade this.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among the people most defiant toward God, may He be praised, is one who kills someone other than his killer, or who kills in the manner of the ignorance of the Jahiliyya, or who kills in the sanctuary of God." [[Ibid.: 15/106.]]

al-Ḍaḥḥak said: This was in Mecca while the Prophet of God (ﷺ) was there, and it was the first thing revealed from the Qur'an concerning killing. The polytheists of Mecca were killing the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). God said: whoever among the polytheists kills you, let his killing you not lead you to kill none but your killer; so do not kill, for the sake of him, a father, a brother, or anyone; if they are from the polytheists, let that not lead you to [...] [unreadable text] so do not kill except your killer. [As in the manuscript.]

This was before Surat Bara'a was revealed and before they were commanded to fight the polytheists.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: it is not accepted [...] upon the number [of killings].

Qatada, Ṭāriq ibn Ḥabīb and Ibn Kaysan said: [the victim] is not to be mutilated.

﴿Indeed he was supported﴾: scholars differed about to whom this pronoun refers. It was said it refers to the heir of the victim: he is the one supported against the killer, so the ruler hands the killer over to him; if he wishes he kills him, if he wishes he pardons him, if he wishes he takes the blood money. This is the view of Qatada.

Others said: the pronoun "whoever" [man] refers to the victim in His saying ﴿and whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, meaning that the victim is supported in this world by retaliation, and in the Hereafter by repentance. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan, except in the best manner until he reaches maturity﴾... [the verse continues] ﴿and fulfil the covenant; indeed the covenant is ever questioned﴾ about it. It was also said its meaning is: it was wrongful.

﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even balance﴾.

The people of Kufa read al-qisṭās with a kasra on the qāf. The rest read it with a fatḥa, and it means the balance, like al-qirṭās. Al-qisṭās means a balance, whether small or large. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/257.]]

Mujahid said: it is justice in Greek (rūmiyya). al-Ḥasan said: it is the steelyard (al-qabbān).

﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome﴾: that is, in its consequence.

[al-Ḥasan said:] It has been related to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: "No man has power over something forbidden and then leaves it, having nothing but fear of God, except that God will replace it for him in the hasty world before the Hereafter with something better for him than that." [[Kanz al-ʿUmmal: 15/787; Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/109.]]

﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾. Qatada said: do not say "I saw" when you did not see, or "I heard" when you did not hear, or "I know" when you do not know. This is a report from ʿAli from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Mujahid said: do not accuse anyone of what you have no knowledge of. This is the narration of ʿAṭiyya from Ibn ʿAbbas. [[See Zad al-Masir of Ibn al-Jawzi: 5/27.]]

Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya said: it is false testimony.

[al-Qutaybi] said: do not follow conjecture and assumptions. All of these are close in meaning. The root of qafw is slander and false accusation. From it comes the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We are the sons of al-Naḍr ibn Kinana; we do not slander our mother, nor do we disown our father." [[al-Mu'jam al-Kabir of al-Tabarani: 1/236; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 1/22, with the wording: "nor do we claim (to be) of other than our father".]]

al-Nabigha said:

"And like statues, of noble noses, dwelling
with them is modesty; they do not wrong with accusations (al-taqāfī)."
[al-Taqafi: accusing, the verse is attributed in Tafsir al-Tabari to some Basran scholars: 15/110.]

al-Kumayt said:

"So I do not hurl at the innocent without fault,
nor do I slander the chaste, when we were slandered."
[As in the manuscript.]

[al-Qutaybi] said: it is derived from the qafa' (back of the head), as if one follows (yaqfū) matters and goes after their backs, and follows them and seeks to know them. It is said: "I followed his trace" (qafawtu athārahu), on the pattern of "I called" (daʿawtu). Its prohibition is: do not follow (lā taqfu), like your saying: do not leave (lā tadaʿ).

al-Farra' related from some people that its origin is from al-qiyafa, which is following a trace. If that is so, then (wa-lā taqfu) must be read with a ḍamma on the qāf and a sukūn on the fā', like (wa-lā taqul). He said: The Arabs say: "I followed her trace" and "I followed (qafat)" like their saying: qā'a al-jamal al-nāqa idhā rakibahā waqʿan (the camel mounted the she-camel), and ʿāth and ʿathan, iʿtāma and iʿtamā, and iḥtāja māluhu and iḥtajā.

The poet said:

"And if I had struck you from close by,
it would have pulled you away from the wolf's cry, the wolf."

That is, it embraced (ʿānaqa). [As in the manuscript.]

﴿Indeed the hearing and the sight and the heart, all of those﴾: that is, all these limbs and organs, will be asked about those [acts].

As in the saying of the poet, Jarir:

"Blame the dwellings after the place of al-Liwā,
and life after those days."
[See Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/111.]

It may also be that the pronoun refers to their owners and possessors.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾: with arrogance, pride and vanity. This explains the walking, not describes it, because this emphasis is put in the form of the verbal noun. ﴿Indeed you will never tear the earth﴾: that is, you will never cut it with your heels until you reach its end. It is said: "So-and-so is more the tearer of the earth than so-and-so" when he travels more and is stronger.

Ruʾba said:

"And a standing one, of the depths, empty of the cut-through"
meaning: the one cut off.

﴿Nor will you reach the mountains in height﴾: that is, you will not equal them in height, nor will your stature reach them. He informed that whoever does this gains nothing from it [...] [unreadable word] from him anything else. ﴿All that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾.

al-Ḥasan, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn ʿUmar and the people of Kufa read sayyi'uhu as an annexed construction (iḍāfa), meaning: all this which we have mentioned, from His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾.

[The reading] "kāna sayyiʾatan" means "it was an evil thing," in respect of what we have mentioned and promised concerning you. ﴿In the sight of your Lord, hateful.﴾ They said: because in what God has mentioned, from His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ up to this point, there are things commanded and things forbidden. The people of Kufa said: it refers to meaning, because sayyi'a is a sin, and it is [not literal]. ﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾, up to His saying ﴿dismissed﴾: cast out, banished from every helper. The intended meaning is other than him.

﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an﴾: the common readers read it with shadd on the ṣād, for intensification. al-Ḥasan read ṣarafnā with tashdīd removed.

﴿In this Qur'an﴾: meaning the lessons, wisdoms, parables, rulings, proofs and signs.

The first: He did not make it one kind, but rather promise and warning, command and prohibition, decisive and ambiguous, abrogating and abrogated, reports and parables, like the diversification of winds: east, west, south and north; and the diversification of verbs from past to future, from active to passive, and the like.

The second: He did not reveal it once, but in installments (nujūman), as in His saying ﴿And a Qur'an We have divided (farraqnāhu)﴾, meaning: We have repeatedly turned Gabriel toward you. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/265.]]

﴿That they may remember (liyadhdhakkarū)﴾. Yaḥyā, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read liyadhkurū without shadd. The rest read it with shadd, and Abu ʿUbayd chose it, meaning: that they may take heed (liyatadhakkarū). ﴿And it increases them only in aversion﴾: fleeing and distancing from the truth.

﴿Say, O Muhammad, to these polytheists: if there were with Him other gods, as they say﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ḥafṣ read yaqūlūna with ya'; the rest with ta'.

﴿Then they would have sought to the Lord of the Throne a way﴾: they would have sought the gods to draw near to Him, seeking nearness to Him.

Qatada said: It means: if the matter were as they say, then they would know God's favor and His nearness to them, so they would do what draws them closer to Him.

Others said: then they would have sought, along with God, contention and fighting, like the kings of the world acting against one another. Then He declared Himself free of what they say, saying ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted far above what they say﴾.

al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i, and Abu ʿUbayd chose it from them, read ta'ālā with the tā' ("ʿulūwan kabīran"), great exaltation, and did not say ta'āliyan, like His saying [wa-ja'ala] to Him a way.

﴿And give the near of kin his due﴾. This means maintaining ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim).

Some said: it refers to the kinship of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Al-Suddi narrated from Ibn al-Daylami who said: ʿAli ibn al-Husayn said to a man from the people of Syria, "Have you recited the Qur'an?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Have you not read in (the chapter of) the Children of Israel: ﴿And give the near of kin his due﴾?" He said, "Are you the near of kin whom God commanded to be given their due?" He said, "Yes."

﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾: the traveller on the road. It was also said: the guest.

﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾: do not spend your wealth in disobedience.

Salama ibn Kuhayl narrated from Abu [ʿUbayda], from Ibn al-Ḍarīr, that he asked Ibn Masʿud, "What is wastefulness (tabdhīr)?"

He said: "Spending wealth in other than its right place." [[Tafsir Mujahid: 1/361.]]

Mujahid said: If a person spent all his wealth in what is right, it would not be wastefulness; but if he spent a single hand's worth in what is false, that would be wastefulness.

Shuʿayb said: I was walking with Abu Ishaq on the road to Kufa when he came upon a house being built with plaster and baked brick, and he said: "This is wastefulness, according to the saying of ʿAbd Allah: spending wealth in other than its right place." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/94.]]

﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾: their helpers and allies. The Arabs say: whoever adheres to the custom of a people and follows their way is their brother. ﴿And Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾: denying the blessings.

It was revealed concerning Munajji, Bilal, Suhayb, Salim and Khabbab. They used to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) from time to time for what they needed, and he did not find anything to give them, so he would turn away from them out of shyness before them.

Then God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾, meaning: if you turn away from these people to whom I ordered you to give their rights when they ask you, and you have nothing to give them, out of shame before them.

﴿Seeking mercy from your Lord﴾: seeking provision from God, which you hope will come to you. ﴿Then speak to them a gentle word﴾: softly, promising them a good promise.

﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, the verse.

Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah said: While the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sitting among the Companions, a boy came to him and said, "O Messenger of God, my mother asks you to clothe her with a garment." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had nothing but his shirt. The boy said, "From one hour to another, it appears there is a delay until another time." So he went back to his mother, who said, "Tell him: my mother asks you for the garment you are wearing." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered his house, took off his shirt, gave it to him, and sat naked. Bilal called the adhan for the prayer, and they waited, but he did not come out. This troubled the hearts of the Companions, so some of them entered upon him and saw him naked. Then God, Exalted, revealed: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾. [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 194.]]

Meaning: do not withhold your hand from spending in what is right, like a hand bound to the neck, which cannot be extended to give.

﴿Nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ in giving, so that you give all that you possess, ﴿and so you sit reproached﴾: your askers will blame you when you do not give them, ﴿and destitute﴾: cut off from you, with nothing left to spend. God said: ﴿Your sight will return to you dazzled while it is weary﴾ [Surat al-Mulk: 4]. Qatada said: regretful for what has passed from you. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/251.]]

This was because the people of ignorance used to bury their daughters alive for fear of poverty, so God forbade them from that and informed them that their provision and the provision of their daughters is upon God, Exalted. ﴿Indeed, their killing has ever been a great sin﴾. Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fatḥa on the kha and the ṭāʾ, with the hamza shortened (khiṭʾan).

Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra on the kha, a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ, and a long hamza (khiṭāʾan).

The rest read it with a kasra on the kha and a sukūn on the ṭāʾ (khiṭan). All these are dialectal forms with one meaning, and the word may be a noun or a verbal noun.

﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾: and by its right, which is what [follows].

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Ḥusayn say, in the presence of the Imam Abu al-Ṭayyib, regarding His saying ṣarrafnā, that it has two meanings. The first: He did not make it one kind, but rather promise and warning, command and prohibition, decisive and ambiguous, abrogating and abrogated, reports and parables, like the diversification of winds: east, west, south and north; and the diversification of verbs from past to future, from active to passive, and the like.

The second: He did not reveal it once, but in installments (nujūman), as in His saying ﴿And a Qur'an We have divided (farraqnāhu)﴾, meaning: We have repeatedly turned Gabriel toward you. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/265.]]

﴿That they may remember (liyadhdhakkarū)﴾. Yaḥyā, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read liyadhkurū without shadd. The rest read it with shadd, and Abu ʿUbayd chose it, meaning: that they may take heed (liyatadhakkarū). ﴿And it increases them only in aversion﴾: fleeing and distancing from the truth.

﴿Say, O Muhammad, to these polytheists: if there were with Him other gods, as they say﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ḥafṣ read yaqūlūna with ya'; the rest with ta'.

﴿Then they would have sought to the Lord of the Throne a way﴾: they would have sought the gods to draw near to Him, seeking nearness to Him.

Qatada said: It means: if the matter were as they say, then they would know God's favor and His nearness to them, so they would do what draws them closer to Him.

Others said: then they would have sought, along with God, contention and fighting, like the kings of the world acting against one another. Then He declared Himself free of what they say, saying ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted far above what they say﴾.

al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i, and Abu ʿUbayd chose it from them, read ta'ālā with the tā' ("ʿulūwan kabīran"), great exaltation, and did not say ta'āliyan, like His saying [wa-ja'ala] to Him a way.

﴿And give the near of kin his due﴾. This means maintaining ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim).

Some said: it refers to the kinship of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Al-Suddi narrated from Ibn al-Daylami who said: ʿAli ibn al-Husayn said to a man from the people of Syria, "Have you recited the Qur'an?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Have you not read in (the chapter of) the Children of Israel: ﴿And give the near of kin his due﴾?" He said, "Are you the near of kin whom God commanded to be given their due?" He said, "Yes."

﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾: the traveller on the road. It was also said: the guest.

﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾: do not spend your wealth in disobedience.

Salama ibn Kuhayl narrated from Abu [ʿUbayda], from Ibn al-Ḍarīr, that he asked Ibn Masʿud, "What is wastefulness (tabdhīr)?"

He said: "Spending wealth in other than its right place." [[Tafsir Mujahid: 1/361.]]

Mujahid said: If a person spent all his wealth in what is right, it would not be wastefulness; but if he spent a single hand's worth in what is false, that would be wastefulness.

Shuʿayb said: I was walking with Abu Ishaq on the road to Kufa when he came upon a house being built with plaster and baked brick, and he said: "This is wastefulness, according to the saying of ʿAbd Allah: spending wealth in other than its right place." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/94.]]

﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾: their helpers and allies. The Arabs say: whoever adheres to the custom of a people and follows their way is their brother. ﴿And Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾: denying the blessings.

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾, the verse.

It was revealed concerning Munajji, Bilal, Suhayb, Salim and Khabbab. They used to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) from time to time for what they needed, and he did not find anything to give them, so he would turn away from them out of shyness before them.

Then God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾, meaning: if you turn away from these people to whom I ordered you to give their rights when they ask you, and you have nothing to give them, out of shame before them.

﴿Seeking mercy from your Lord﴾: seeking provision from God, which you hope will come to you. ﴿Then speak to them a gentle word﴾: softly, promising them a good promise.

﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, the verse.

Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah said: While the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sitting among the Companions, a boy came to him and said, "O Messenger of God, my mother asks you to clothe her with a garment." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had nothing but his shirt. The boy said, "From one hour to another, it appears there is a delay until another time." So he went back to his mother, who said, "Tell him: my mother asks you for the garment you are wearing." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered his house, took off his shirt, gave it to him, and sat naked. Bilal called the adhan for the prayer, and they waited, but he did not come out. This troubled the hearts of the Companions, so some of them entered upon him and saw him naked. Then God, Exalted, revealed: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾. [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 194.]]

Meaning: do not withhold your hand from spending in what is right, like a hand bound to the neck, which cannot be extended to give.

﴿Nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ in giving, so that you give all that you possess, ﴿and so you sit reproached﴾: your askers will blame you when you do not give them, ﴿and destitute﴾: cut off from you, with nothing left to spend. It is said: "He was exhausted (ḥasara) by the request," when it wearied him. A beast is ḥasīr when it is weary and exhausted. And ḥasīr of sight is when it is tired. God said: ﴿Your sight will return to you dazzled while it is weary﴾ [Surat al-Mulk: 4]. Qatada said: regretful for what has passed from you. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/251.]]

﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾: He widens and narrows. ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿If God had extended provision to His servants, they would have committed excess upon the earth﴾, the verse. [Here the text reads "wa-law wassaʿa" as in the manuscript.]

﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾: destitution and scarcity. ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾. This was because the people of ignorance used to bury their daughters alive for fear of poverty, so God forbade them from that and informed them that their provision and the provision of their daughters is upon God, Exalted. ﴿Indeed, their killing has ever been a great sin﴾. The readers differed concerning it:

Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fatḥa on the kha and the ṭāʾ, with the hamza shortened (khiṭʾan).

Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra on the kha, a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ, and a long hamza (khiṭāʾan).

The rest read it with a kasra on the kha and a sukūn on the ṭāʾ (khiṭan). All these are dialectal forms with one meaning, and the word may be a noun or a verbal noun.

﴿And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse; indeed it is ever an immorality and an evil way﴾.

﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾: and by its right, which is what [follows].

Humayd narrated from Anas who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say: there is no god but God. When they say it, their blood and their property are protected from me, except by its right, and their reckoning is with God." It was said: What is its right? He said: "Adultery after being married, apostasy after faith, and killing a soul, so that he is killed in retaliation for it." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/103.]]

﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾: power and authority over the killer of his heir. If he wishes, he may take retaliation; if he wishes, he may pardon him; if he wishes, he may take blood money, which God has made lawful. ﴿But let him not commit excess in killing﴾. Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with the letter ta' (tusrif), meaning: do not commit excess, O killer. It is also possible that the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), with the intended meaning being the leaders and the community after him. Whoever reads it with ya' refers it to the heir (al-mawlā).

They differed about what excess is. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he should not kill anyone other than his killer.

al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: In the days of ignorance, when one of the Arabs was killed, they would not be content to kill the killer of their companion until they had killed someone more noble than the one who had killed him. So the heir of the victim would go to a noble man of the killer's tribe and kill him in exchange for his heir, leaving the killer alive. God forbade this.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among the people most defiant toward God, may He be praised, is one who kills someone other than his killer, or who kills in the manner of the ignorance of the Jahiliyya, or who kills in the sanctuary of God." [[Ibid.: 15/106.]]

al-Ḍaḥḥak said: This was in Mecca while the Prophet of God (ﷺ) was there, and it was the first thing revealed from the Qur'an concerning killing. The polytheists of Mecca were killing the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). God said: whoever among the polytheists kills you, let his killing you not lead you to kill none but your killer; so do not kill, for the sake of him, a father, a brother, or anyone; if they are from the polytheists, let that not lead you to [...] [unreadable text] so do not kill except your killer. [As in the manuscript.]

This was before Surat Bara'a was revealed and before they were commanded to fight the polytheists.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: it is not accepted [...] upon the number [of killings].

Qatada, Ṭāriq ibn Ḥabīb and Ibn Kaysan said: [the victim] is not to be mutilated.

﴿Indeed he was supported﴾: scholars differed about to whom this pronoun refers. It was said it refers to the heir of the victim: he is the one supported against the killer, so the ruler hands the killer over to him; if he wishes he kills him, if he wishes he pardons him, if he wishes he takes the blood money. This is the view of Qatada.

Others said: the pronoun "whoever" [man] refers to the victim in His saying ﴿and whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, meaning that the victim is supported in this world by retaliation, and in the Hereafter by repentance. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan, except in the best manner until he reaches maturity﴾... [the verse continues] ﴿and fulfil the covenant; indeed the covenant is ever questioned﴾ about it. It was also said its meaning is: it was wrongful.

﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even balance﴾.

The people of Kufa read al-qisṭās with a kasra on the qāf. The rest read it with a fatḥa, and it means the balance, like al-qirṭās. Al-qisṭās means a balance, whether small or large. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/257.]]

Mujahid said: it is justice in Greek (rūmiyya). al-Ḥasan said: it is the steelyard (al-qabbān).

﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome﴾: that is, in its consequence.

[al-Ḥasan said:] It has been related to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: "No man has power over something forbidden and then leaves it, having nothing but fear of God, except that God will replace it for him in the hasty world before the Hereafter with something better for him than that." [[Kanz al-ʿUmmal: 15/787; Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/109.]]

﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾. Qatada said: do not say "I saw" when you did not see, or "I heard" when you did not hear, or "I know" when you do not know. This is a report from ʿAli from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Mujahid said: do not accuse anyone of what you have no knowledge of. This is the narration of ʿAṭiyya from Ibn ʿAbbas. [[See Zad al-Masir of Ibn al-Jawzi: 5/27.]]

Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya said: it is false testimony.

[al-Qutaybi] said: do not follow conjecture and assumptions. All of these are close in meaning. The root of qafw is slander and false accusation. From it comes the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We are the sons of al-Naḍr ibn Kinana; we do not slander our mother, nor do we disown our father." [[al-Mu'jam al-Kabir of al-Tabarani: 1/236; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 1/22, with the wording: "nor do we claim (to be) of other than our father".]]

al-Nabigha said:

"And like statues, of noble noses, dwelling
with them is modesty; they do not wrong with accusations (al-taqāfī)."
[al-Taqafi: accusing, the verse is attributed in Tafsir al-Tabari to some Basran scholars: 15/110.]

al-Kumayt said:

"So I do not hurl at the innocent without fault,
nor do I slander the chaste, when we were slandered."
[As in the manuscript.]

[al-Qutaybi] said: it is derived from the qafa' (back of the head), as if one follows (yaqfū) matters and goes after their backs, and follows them and seeks to know them. It is said: "I followed his trace" (qafawtu athārahu), on the pattern of "I called" (daʿawtu). Its prohibition is: do not follow (lā taqfu), like your saying: do not leave (lā tadaʿ).

al-Farra' related from some people that its origin is from al-qiyafa, which is following a trace. If that is so, then (wa-lā taqfu) must be read with a ḍamma on the qāf and a sukūn on the fā', like (wa-lā taqul). He said: The Arabs say: "I followed her trace" and "I followed (qafat)" like their saying: qā'a al-jamal al-nāqa idhā rakibahā waqʿan (the camel mounted the she-camel), and ʿāth and ʿathan, iʿtāma and iʿtamā, and iḥtāja māluhu and iḥtajā.

The poet said:

"And if I had struck you from close by,
it would have pulled you away from the wolf's cry, the wolf."

That is, it embraced (ʿānaqa). [As in the manuscript.]

﴿Indeed the hearing and the sight and the heart, all of those﴾: that is, all these limbs and organs, will be asked about those [acts].

As in the saying of the poet, Jarir:

"Blame the dwellings after the place of al-Liwā,
and life after those days."
[See Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/111.]

It may also be that the pronoun refers to their owners and possessors.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾: with arrogance, pride and vanity. This explains the walking, not describes it, because this emphasis is put in the form of the verbal noun. ﴿Indeed you will never tear the earth﴾: that is, you will never cut it with your heels until you reach its end. It is said: "So-and-so is more the tearer of the earth than so-and-so" when he travels more and is stronger.

Ruʾba said:

"And a standing one, of the depths, empty of the cut-through"
meaning: the one cut off.

﴿Nor will you reach the mountains in height﴾: that is, you will not equal them in height, nor will your stature reach them. He informed that whoever does this gains nothing from it [...] [unreadable word] from him anything else. ﴿All that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾.

al-Ḥasan, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn ʿUmar and the people of Kufa read sayyi'uhu as an annexed construction (iḍāfa), meaning: all this which we have mentioned, from His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾.

[The reading] "kāna sayyiʾatan" means "it was an evil thing," in respect of what we have mentioned and promised concerning you. ﴿In the sight of your Lord, hateful.﴾ They said: because in what God has mentioned, from His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ up to this point, there are things commanded and things forbidden. Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading for the meaning mentioned, and because in the reading of Abu Ḥajja, which Abu ʿUbayd related from Ḥajjāj from Hārūn, in the reading of [Ubayy ibn Kaʿb]: (kāna sayyi'ātuhu), he said: this would be by annexing an indefinite accusative sayyi'a, meaning: all that which we have mentioned and promised from His saying ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ up to this point was an evil thing, not a good thing. So they made "kull" comprehensive of what is forbidden and nothing else. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/262.]]

If it is said: why did you not make makrūhan a second predicate? We say: there is a fronting and deferment in the speech; its intended sense is: all that was hateful and evil. It was said: it is an act [...] like a substitute, not as a description; the meaning: all that was evil and was hateful.

The people of Kufa said: it refers to meaning, because sayyi'a is a sin, and it is [not literal]. ﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾, up to His saying ﴿dismissed﴾: cast out, banished from every helper. The intended meaning is other than him.

al-Kalbi said: the eighteen [commandments] were verses in the tablets of Moses, and they are ten verses in the Torah.

﴿Has your Lord then preferred you with sons and taken from the angels females?﴾ — chosen you and singled you out. ﴿Indeed you are saying a grave saying﴾: addressing the polytheists of the Arabs, when they said: the angels are the daughters of God.

al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: In the days of ignorance, when one of the Arabs was killed, they would not be content to kill the killer of their companion until they had killed someone more noble than the one who had killed him. So the heir of the victim would go to a noble man of the killer's tribe and kill him in exchange for his heir, leaving the killer alive. God forbade this.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Among the people most defiant toward God, may He be praised, is one who kills someone other than his killer, or who kills in the manner of the ignorance of the Jahiliyya, or who kills in the sanctuary of God." [[Ibid.: 15/106.]]

al-Ḍaḥḥak said: This was in Mecca while the Prophet of God (ﷺ) was there, and it was the first thing revealed from the Qur'an concerning killing. The polytheists of Mecca were killing the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). God said: whoever among the polytheists kills you, let his killing you not lead you to kill none but your killer; so do not kill, for the sake of him, a father, a brother, or anyone; if they are from the polytheists, let that not lead you to [...] [unreadable text] so do not kill except your killer. [As in the manuscript.]

This was before Surat Bara'a was revealed and before they were commanded to fight the polytheists.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: it is not accepted [...] upon the number [of killings].

Qatada, Ṭāriq ibn Ḥabīb and Ibn Kaysan said: [the victim] is not to be mutilated.

﴿Indeed he was supported﴾: scholars differed about to whom this pronoun refers. It was said it refers to the heir of the victim: he is the one supported against the killer, so the ruler hands the killer over to him; if he wishes he kills him, if he wishes he pardons him, if he wishes he takes the blood money. This is the view of Qatada.

Others said: the pronoun "whoever" [man] refers to the victim in His saying ﴿and whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, meaning that the victim is supported in this world by retaliation, and in the Hereafter by repentance. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿And do not approach the property of an orphan, except in the best manner until he reaches maturity﴾... [the verse continues] ﴿and fulfil the covenant; indeed the covenant is ever questioned﴾ about it. It was also said its meaning is: it was wrongful.

﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even balance﴾.

The people of Kufa read al-qisṭās with a kasra on the qāf. The rest read it with a fatḥa, and it means the balance, like al-qirṭās. Al-qisṭās means a balance, whether small or large. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/257.]]

Mujahid said: it is justice in Greek (rūmiyya). al-Ḥasan said: it is the steelyard (al-qabbān).

﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome﴾: that is, in its consequence.

[al-Ḥasan said:] It has been related to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: "No man has power over something forbidden and then leaves it, having nothing but fear of God, except that God will replace it for him in the hasty world before the Hereafter with something better for him than that." [[Kanz al-ʿUmmal: 15/787; Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/109.]]

﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾. Qatada said: do not say "I saw" when you did not see, or "I heard" when you did not hear, or "I know" when you do not know. This is a report from ʿAli from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Mujahid said: do not accuse anyone of what you have no knowledge of. This is the narration of ʿAṭiyya from Ibn ʿAbbas. [[See Zad al-Masir of Ibn al-Jawzi: 5/27.]]

Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya said: it is false testimony.

[al-Qutaybi] said: do not follow conjecture and assumptions. All of these are close in meaning. The root of qafw is slander and false accusation. From it comes the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We are the sons of al-Naḍr ibn Kinana; we do not slander our mother, nor do we disown our father." [[al-Mu'jam al-Kabir of al-Tabarani: 1/236; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 1/22, with the wording: "nor do we claim (to be) of other than our father".]]

al-Nabigha said:

"And like statues, of noble noses, dwelling
with them is modesty; they do not wrong with accusations (al-taqāfī)."
[al-Taqafi: accusing, the verse is attributed in Tafsir al-Tabari to some Basran scholars: 15/110.]

al-Kumayt said:

"So I do not hurl at the innocent without fault,
nor do I slander the chaste, when we were slandered."
[As in the manuscript.]

[al-Qutaybi] said: it is derived from the qafa' (back of the head), as if one follows (yaqfū) matters and goes after their backs, and follows them and seeks to know them. It is said: "I followed his trace" (qafawtu athārahu), on the pattern of "I called" (daʿawtu). Its prohibition is: do not follow (lā taqfu), like your saying: do not leave (lā tadaʿ).

al-Farra' related from some people that its origin is from al-qiyafa, which is following a trace. If that is so, then (wa-lā taqfu) must be read with a ḍamma on the qāf and a sukūn on the fā', like (wa-lā taqul). He said: The Arabs say: "I followed her trace" and "I followed (qafat)" like their saying: qā'a al-jamal al-nāqa idhā rakibahā waqʿan (the camel mounted the she-camel), and ʿāth and ʿathan, iʿtāma and iʿtamā, and iḥtāja māluhu and iḥtajā.

The poet said:

"And if I had struck you from close by,
it would have pulled you away from the wolf's cry, the wolf."

That is, it embraced (ʿānaqa). [As in the manuscript.]

﴿Indeed the hearing and the sight and the heart, all of those﴾: that is, all these limbs and organs, will be asked about those [acts].

As in the saying of the poet, Jarir:

"Blame the dwellings after the place of al-Liwā,
and life after those days."
[See Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/111.]

It may also be that the pronoun refers to their owners and possessors.

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾: with arrogance, pride and vanity. This explains the walking, not describes it, because this emphasis is put in the form of the verbal noun. ﴿Indeed you will never tear the earth﴾: that is, you will never cut it with your heels until you reach its end. It is said: "So-and-so is more the tearer of the earth than so-and-so" when he travels more and is stronger.

Ruʾba said:

"And a standing one, of the depths, empty of the cut-through"
meaning: the one cut off.

﴿Nor will you reach the mountains in height﴾: that is, you will not equal them in height, nor will your stature reach them. He informed that whoever does this gains nothing from it [...] [unreadable word] from him anything else. ﴿All that — its evil is hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾.

al-Ḥasan, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, Ibn ʿUmar and the people of Kufa read sayyi'uhu as an annexed construction (iḍāfa), meaning: all this which we have mentioned, from His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾.

[The reading] "kāna sayyiʾatan" means "it was an evil thing," in respect of what we have mentioned and promised concerning you. ﴿In the sight of your Lord, hateful.﴾ They said: because in what God has mentioned, from His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ up to this point, there are things commanded and things forbidden. Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading for the meaning mentioned, and because in the reading of Abu Ḥajja, which Abu ʿUbayd related from Ḥajjāj from Hārūn, in the reading of [Ubayy ibn Kaʿb]: (kāna sayyi'ātuhu), he said: this would be by annexing an indefinite accusative sayyi'a, meaning: all that which we have mentioned and promised from His saying ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ up to this point was an evil thing, not a good thing. So they made "kull" comprehensive of what is forbidden and nothing else. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/262.]]

If it is said: why did you not make makrūhan a second predicate? We say: there is a fronting and deferment in the speech; its intended sense is: all that was hateful and evil. It was said: it is an act [...] like a substitute, not as a description; the meaning: all that was evil and was hateful.

The people of Kufa said: it refers to meaning, because sayyi'a is a sin, and it is [not literal]. ﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾, up to His saying ﴿dismissed﴾: cast out, banished from every helper. The intended meaning is other than him.

al-Kalbi said: the eighteen [commandments] were verses in the tablets of Moses, and they are ten verses in the Torah.

﴿Has your Lord then preferred you with sons and taken from the angels females?﴾ — chosen you and singled you out. ﴿Indeed you are saying a grave saying﴾: addressing the polytheists of the Arabs, when they said: the angels are the daughters of God.

﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an﴾: the common readers read it with shadd on the ṣād, for intensification. al-Ḥasan read ṣarafnā with tashdīd removed.

﴿In this Qur'an﴾: meaning the lessons, wisdoms, parables, rulings, proofs and signs.

I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Ḥusayn say, in the presence of the Imam Abu al-Ṭayyib, regarding His saying ṣarrafnā, that it has two meanings. The first: He did not make it one kind, but rather promise and warning, command and prohibition, decisive and ambiguous, abrogating and abrogated, reports and parables, like the diversification of winds: east, west, south and north; and the diversification of verbs from past to future, from active to passive, and the like.

The second: He did not reveal it once, but in installments (nujūman), as in His saying ﴿And a Qur'an We have divided (farraqnāhu)﴾, meaning: We have repeatedly turned Gabriel toward you. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/265.]]

﴿That they may remember (liyadhdhakkarū)﴾. Yaḥyā, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read liyadhkurū without shadd. The rest read it with shadd, and Abu ʿUbayd chose it, meaning: that they may take heed (liyatadhakkarū). ﴿And it increases them only in aversion﴾: fleeing and distancing from the truth.

﴿Say, O Muhammad, to these polytheists: if there were with Him other gods, as they say﴾.

Ibn Kathir and Ḥafṣ read yaqūlūna with ya'; the rest with ta'.

﴿Then they would have sought to the Lord of the Throne a way﴾: they would have sought the gods to draw near to Him, seeking nearness to Him.

Qatada said: It means: if the matter were as they say, then they would know God's favor and His nearness to them, so they would do what draws them closer to Him.

Others said: then they would have sought, along with God, contention and fighting, like the kings of the world acting against one another. Then He declared Himself free of what they say, saying ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted far above what they say﴾.

al-Aʿmash, Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i, and Abu ʿUbayd chose it from them, read ta'ālā with the tā' ("ʿulūwan kabīran"), great exaltation, and did not say ta'āliyan, like His saying [wa-ja'ala] to Him a way.

﴿And give the near of kin his due﴾. This means maintaining ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim).

Some said: it refers to the kinship of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Al-Suddi narrated from Ibn al-Daylami who said: ʿAli ibn al-Husayn said to a man from the people of Syria, "Have you recited the Qur'an?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Have you not read in (the chapter of) the Children of Israel: ﴿And give the near of kin his due﴾?" He said, "Are you the near of kin whom God commanded to be given their due?" He said, "Yes."

﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾: the traveller on the road. It was also said: the guest.

﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾: do not spend your wealth in disobedience.

Salama ibn Kuhayl narrated from Abu [ʿUbayda], from Ibn al-Ḍarīr, that he asked Ibn Masʿud, "What is wastefulness (tabdhīr)?"

He said: "Spending wealth in other than its right place." [[Tafsir Mujahid: 1/361.]]

Mujahid said: If a person spent all his wealth in what is right, it would not be wastefulness; but if he spent a single hand's worth in what is false, that would be wastefulness.

Shuʿayb said: I was walking with Abu Ishaq on the road to Kufa when he came upon a house being built with plaster and baked brick, and he said: "This is wastefulness, according to the saying of ʿAbd Allah: spending wealth in other than its right place." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/94.]]

﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾: their helpers and allies. The Arabs say: whoever adheres to the custom of a people and follows their way is their brother. ﴿And Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾: denying the blessings.

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾, the verse.

It was revealed concerning Munajji, Bilal, Suhayb, Salim and Khabbab. They used to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) from time to time for what they needed, and he did not find anything to give them, so he would turn away from them out of shyness before them.

Then God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾, meaning: if you turn away from these people to whom I ordered you to give their rights when they ask you, and you have nothing to give them, out of shame before them.

﴿Seeking mercy from your Lord﴾: seeking provision from God, which you hope will come to you. ﴿Then speak to them a gentle word﴾: softly, promising them a good promise.

﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾, the verse.

Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah said: While the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sitting among the Companions, a boy came to him and said, "O Messenger of God, my mother asks you to clothe her with a garment." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) had nothing but his shirt. The boy said, "From one hour to another, it appears there is a delay until another time." So he went back to his mother, who said, "Tell him: my mother asks you for the garment you are wearing." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered his house, took off his shirt, gave it to him, and sat naked. Bilal called the adhan for the prayer, and they waited, but he did not come out. This troubled the hearts of the Companions, so some of them entered upon him and saw him naked. Then God, Exalted, revealed: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾. [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 194.]]

Meaning: do not withhold your hand from spending in what is right, like a hand bound to the neck, which cannot be extended to give.

﴿Nor extend it fully outstretched﴾ in giving, so that you give all that you possess, ﴿and so you sit reproached﴾: your askers will blame you when you do not give them, ﴿and destitute﴾: cut off from you, with nothing left to spend. It is said: "He was exhausted (ḥasara) by the request," when it wearied him. A beast is ḥasīr when it is weary and exhausted. And ḥasīr of sight is when it is tired. God said: ﴿Your sight will return to you dazzled while it is weary﴾ [Surat al-Mulk: 4]. Qatada said: regretful for what has passed from you. [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 10/251.]]

﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾: He widens and narrows. ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿If God had extended provision to His servants, they would have committed excess upon the earth﴾, the verse. [Here the text reads "wa-law wassaʿa" as in the manuscript.]

﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾: destitution and scarcity. ﴿We provide for them and for you﴾. This was because the people of ignorance used to bury their daughters alive for fear of poverty, so God forbade them from that and informed them that their provision and the provision of their daughters is upon God, Exalted. ﴿Indeed, their killing has ever been a great sin﴾. The readers differed concerning it:

Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿAmir read it with a fatḥa on the kha and the ṭāʾ, with the hamza shortened (khiṭʾan).

Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra on the kha, a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ, and a long hamza (khiṭāʾan).

The rest read it with a kasra on the kha and a sukūn on the ṭāʾ (khiṭan). All these are dialectal forms with one meaning, and the word may be a noun or a verbal noun.

﴿And do not approach unlawful sexual intercourse; indeed it is ever an immorality and an evil way﴾.

﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾: and by its right, which is what [follows].

Humayd narrated from Anas who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to fight the people until they say: there is no god but God. When they say it, their blood and their property are protected from me, except by its right, and their reckoning is with God." It was said: What is its right? He said: "Adultery after being married, apostasy after faith, and killing a soul, so that he is killed in retaliation for it." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 15/103.]]

﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority﴾: power and authority over the killer of his heir. If he wishes, he may take retaliation; if he wishes, he may pardon him; if he wishes, he may take blood money, which God has made lawful. ﴿But let him not commit excess in killing﴾. Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with the letter ta' (tusrif), meaning: do not commit excess, O killer. It is also possible that the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), with the intended meaning being the leaders and the community after him. Whoever reads it with ya' refers it to the heir (al-mawlā).

They differed about what excess is. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he should not kill anyone other than his killer.
